name: Pig collagen

lead: Pig collagen is collagen protein from porcine skin, found in Korean sheet masks and creams and taken as a supplement. People use it for plumper, smoother-looking, better-hydrated skin.

The idea is that collagen in a mask or cream hydrates the surface so skin looks fuller. Wikipedia notes that intact collagen is too large to enter skin, so many cosmetics use hydrolysed peptides, and that as of 2025 it reports no clinical evidence for topical or oral collagen against wrinkles. Porcine collagen itself is used in wound dressings and dental and surgical membranes.

paras: Most people use it as a sheet mask or cream applied to the face as part of a hydration routine, often several times a week. Supplement versions are taken by mouth alongside other skincare. Any plumping from a mask is usually a surface-hydration effect that shows up right after use.
As a pork-derived product it may not suit people who avoid pork. Porcine tissue has triggered immune responses in transplant research. No cosmetic safety data were found for masks or creams.

angle.text: Pig collagen goes into Korean sheet masks and creams, and into supplements, so skin is hydrated at the surface and looks plumper and smoother. Porcine collagen has established surgical uses, while cosmetic trials of masks have not been published.

lead: Pig (porcine) collagen is collagen protein derived from pig skin or connective tissue. In beauty it appears in sheet masks and creams, particularly in Korean products, and as a supplement; in medicine, porcine collagen is used in wound dressings and dental and surgical membranes.[1][2]

Wikipedia states that intact collagen is too large to penetrate skin when applied topically, that cosmetics therefore often use hydrolysed forms, and that as of 2025 no clinical evidence supports oral or topical collagen products for wrinkles or skin ageing.[1] Proponents of collagen products hold that they hydrate or firm skin.

paras: Collagen creams are sold as cosmetics, but according to Wikipedia intact collagen fibres cannot enter the skin, and low-molecular-weight hydrolysed forms are used on the unproven belief they absorb better. Ingested collagen is digested to peptides and amino acids.[1] A surface film of collagen may act as a humectant, but this role was not assessed in the sources reviewed.

Porcine collagen has been studied as a biomaterial, including porcine tendon grafts treated to remove alpha-gal epitopes,[3] collagen-coated tracheal prostheses in dogs,[4] and porcine collagen membranes and matrices in dental and wound trials.[5][6] These concern surgical and wound-care applications, not cosmetic masks.

No studies found on pig collagen in cosmetic masks or for appearance. Registered trials involve medical uses such as wound dressings, gingival recession and Mohs surgery wounds.[5][6] A 1965 immunology study examined relationships among animal collagens.[7]
